title: Chipotle Pulls Jalapeños From Restaurants After 110 Salmonella Cases Linked to Peppers in Minnesota
excerpt: The chain's stock dropped nearly 10% as health officials probe contaminated jalapeños served across multiple Mexican-style restaurant chains.
body:
• Minnesota health officials identified 110 cases of Salmonella Javiana tied to jalapeño peppers served at Chipotle and other Mexican-style restaurants between mid-June and mid-July.
  • Among 84 people interviewed, 89% reported eating at Chipotle, though officials said contaminated peppers were likely served at multiple restaurant chains.
  • Chipotle removed the suspected jalapeños from all affected restaurants and replaced them with peppers from different growers.
  • Chipotle shares fell as much as 10% on Tuesday — their largest single-day drop since October — as investors reacted to yet another food safety headline for the chain.

Chipotle Mexican Grill is back in the food safety spotlight after Minnesota health officials linked jalapeño peppers to a salmonella outbreak that has sickened at least 110 people across the state, triggering a sharp stock selloff and a federal traceback investigation.

What Happened

The Minnesota Department of Health on Tuesday confirmed it was investigating an outbreak of Salmonella Javiana associated with jalapeños served at Mexican-style quick-service restaurants. Of the 84 people health officials were able to interview after they fell ill, 75 — or 89% — reported eating at Chipotle between June 14 and July 14.

The remaining cases involved other Mexican-style restaurants, and officials stressed that the contaminated ingredient was not unique to Chipotle. "Based on all the evidence so far, the food that made people sick was served at other restaurants as well," said Carlota Medus, senior epidemiologist supervisor in the department's Foodborne Diseases Unit.

Chipotle's Response

The company said it activated its ingredient traceability system immediately after learning of the potential outbreak and identified jalapeños from a specific lot as a likely common ingredient. It pulled the peppers from every restaurant that had received them and replaced them with product from different growers.

"We have a robust ingredient traceability system," said Laurie Schalow, Chipotle's chief corporate affairs and food safety officer. The company declined to identify its jalapeño supplier.

Minnesota officials said Chipotle had been fully cooperative throughout the investigation and that they were no longer concerned about ongoing exposure at the chain's restaurants. However, they cautioned it was "too soon to know if the outbreak is ongoing" since contaminated peppers may still be in circulation at other food service outlets.

Market Impact

Wall Street's reaction was swift and severe. Chipotle shares dropped as much as 10% on Tuesday to $35.20, their steepest intraday decline since October. The selloff reflected investors' lingering sensitivity to food safety headlines involving the chain, which paid a $25 million fine in 2020 to resolve criminal charges stemming from a series of outbreaks between 2015 and 2018.

The timing compounds an already difficult summer for the restaurant industry. A separate and more widespread cyclosporiasis outbreak linked to shredded iceberg lettuce at Taco Bell locations has sickened thousands across multiple states, demonstrating how quickly contamination scares can dent both consumer confidence and restaurant traffic.

What's Next

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration is leading a traceback investigation to identify the source farm or distributor responsible for the contaminated jalapeños. Until that work concludes, the full scope of the outbreak — and whether it extends beyond Minnesota — remains unclear. The CDC has confirmed thousands of foodborne illness cases across the country this summer, making 2026 one of the worst years on record for restaurant-linked outbreaks.
